posts.title: US Passport Photo Requirements 2026: Size, Background & Rules
posts.excerpt: Everything you need to get a US passport photo accepted — exact dimensions, background, expression and the latest glasses rule.
posts.author: PhotoGov Team
posts.body:
The US passport photo has some of the strictest, most frequently cited rules in the world. Here's the checklist we use in the US passport photo tool so your application isn't delayed.

Exact size

Your photo must be 2×2 inches (51×51 mm), square, with the head centered. Digitally it should be 600×600 pixels at 300 DPI for online applications.

Background

Use a plain white or off-white background with no shadows, patterns or objects. Our one-click white background makes this easy.

Face & expression

  • Face the camera directly, neutral expression, both eyes open.
  • No smiling with teeth showing for the standard photo.
  • Head should fill most of the frame; eye line roughly 1/2 to 2/3 from the top.

Glasses & headwear

Glasses are no longer allowed in US passport photos unless you have a documented medical exemption. Hats and head coverings are only permitted for religious reasons and must not obscure the face.

Tip: take the photo in even, soft lighting — a plain wall and natural daylight works best.

posts.title: How to Take a Passport Photo at Home with Your Phone
posts.excerpt: No studio, no appointment. A simple setup that gets you a compliant photo using just your phone and a wall.
posts.author: PhotoGov Team
posts.body:
You don't need a photo booth. With a phone and a few minutes you can produce a photo that meets official specs.

What you need

  • A friend to hold the phone, or a tripod.
  • A plain wall (white or light grey) and natural daylight.
  • Even lighting — avoid overhead shadows on your face.

Shooting

  1. Stand about arm's length from the wall to avoid a shadow halo.
  2. Hold the camera at eye level, looking straight at the lens.
  3. Keep a neutral expression and remove glasses.
  4. Take a few shots so you can pick the best one.

Finishing

Upload the best shot to PhotoGov, pick your document, and we crop to the exact size and drop in a compliant background. Export as JPG for online forms or PDF for printing.

posts.title: DV Lottery Photo: 6 Common Reasons Applications Get Rejected
posts.excerpt: The Diversity Visa photo rules are strict and a bad photo can disqualify your entry. Avoid these six mistakes.
posts.author: PhotoGov Team
posts.body:
For the US Diversity Visa (green card lottery), a non-compliant photo can get your entire entry disqualified — no second chances. Use our DV Lottery photo tool and watch out for these errors.

1. Wrong dimensions

The photo must be exactly 2×2 inches (600×600 pixels), square. Cropping too tight or leaving a border fails the check.

2. Busy or colored background

Only a plain white background is accepted. No walls with pictures, no shadows.

3. Glasses or hats

Glasses are not allowed, and head coverings (except religious) will be rejected.

4. Poor head position

The head must be centered and facing forward, eyes open, looking at the camera.

5. Old photo

The image must have been taken within the last 6 months.

6. Low resolution or heavy filters

Avoid heavy retouching, filters or blurry images. Keep it natural and sharp.

posts.title: UK Passport Photo Rules Explained
posts.excerpt: The UK uses a 35×45 mm format with its own digital rules. Here's what the HM Passport Office looks for.
posts.author: PhotoGov Team
posts.body:
UK passport photos follow the 35×45 mm format common across Europe, but with specific digital requirements set by HM Passport Office.

Size & crop

Printed size is 35×45 mm. The head must be between 29 mm and 34 mm from chin to crown. Our UK passport photo tool applies these automatically.

Background & lighting

Use a plain light-grey or cream background, evenly lit, no shadows. A neutral expression with a closed mouth is required.

Digital submission

When applying online you upload the digital photo directly — it's analyzed for size, background and face position. Make sure there's no red-eye and the eyes are clearly visible.

posts.title: Visa Photo vs Passport Photo: What's the Difference?
posts.excerpt: They look similar but embassies often have distinct specs. Learn when you can reuse a photo and when you can't.
posts.author: PhotoGov Team
posts.body:
Passport and visa photos often share the same size, but not always. Here's how to avoid a mismatch.

When they're the same

Many countries use the identical format for both — for example the US 2×2 inch photo works for both the passport and most US visas.

When they differ

  • Some visas require a specific size (e.g. Schengen visa uses 35×45 mm; certain Asian visas use 33×45 mm or 35×45 mm).
  • Background color can differ between a passport (often white) and a visa (sometimes light blue).
  • Newer passport photos may ban glasses while a visa application still permits them.

Best practice

Always generate the photo for the specific document you're submitting. Use the document selector in PhotoGov to switch specs in one click rather than reusing an old file.

posts.title: Baby & Child Passport Photos: A Parent's Guide
posts.excerpt: Getting a compliant photo of a wiggly toddler is tricky. Practical tricks to meet the rules for infants and young children.
posts.author: PhotoGov Team
posts.body:
Infant and child passport photos follow the same size rules as adults, but the execution is harder. Here's how parents get it right.

Mouth & eyes

Babies under one don't need a neutral expression, but eyes should be open and the mouth not wide open. For older children, a neutral expression is expected.

The blanket trick

Lay your baby on a plain white sheet and shoot from above — the sheet becomes a compliant background. Remove hats and headbands.

Toys & hands

No toys, dummies or helping hands in the frame. Someone can stand behind the camera and attract attention without appearing in the shot.

Upload to PhotoGov and we'll crop to the exact size and clean up the background.

posts.title: Why Your Passport Photo Gets Rejected — and How to Avoid It
posts.excerpt: The most common rejection reasons, and the quick fixes that keep your application moving.
posts.author: PhotoGov Team
posts.body:
Most rejections come down to a handful of avoidable issues. Run through this list before you submit.

Top rejection reasons

  1. Shadow behind the head or on the background.
  2. Head too large or too small in the frame.
  3. Uneven lighting or red-eye.
  4. Glasses glare or frames cutting the eyes.
  5. Non-compliant background color.

Quick fixes

  • Shoot against a plain wall in soft daylight.
  • Use PhotoGov's one-click background and brightness/contrast sliders.
  • Keep the head centered and let the editor guide eye level.
When in doubt, check the official source linked on the document page — rules change.

posts.title: ID Photo Sizes Around the World
posts.excerpt: A quick tour of the most common ID photo formats — from 35×45 mm in Europe to 2×2 inch in the Americas.
posts.author: PhotoGov Team
posts.body:
ID and document photos come in a surprising variety of sizes. Here are the formats you'll meet most often.

35×45 mm — Europe & many others

The European standard used for passports, IDs and residence permits across the EU, UK, and much of Asia and Africa.

2×2 inch (51×51 mm) — United States

Used for US passports, many US visas and the DV Lottery (600×600 px).

33×45 mm — parts of Asia

Several Asian countries (e.g. some visa types in China, India) use this near-square format.

25×30 mm / 35×35 mm — small IDs

Found on some national ID cards and permits. PhotoGov stores each document's exact size, so you never have to memorize them — just pick the document.
